title: Minimum Substring Partition of Equal Character Frequency
statement:
A string is **balanced** when all of the different letters in it appear equally often.

Split `s` into one or more non-empty contiguous substrings that, kept in their original order, make up the whole of `s`, so that every substring is balanced. Return the smallest number of substrings such a split can use. A split always exists, because any single character is balanced.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every way to cut the string is exponential. Look at the last piece instead: if it is `s[start..end)` and it is balanced, the cost is one more than the best split of the first `start` letters. So the answer for every prefix follows from shorter prefixes, a 1-D DP.

To test whether `s[start..end)` is balanced in O(1), grow the piece leftwards one letter at a time and keep its letter counts. The piece is balanced exactly when (largest count) × (number of distinct letters) equals its length: the counts sum to the length and none exceeds the largest, so equality means they are all the same.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[i]` be the fewest pieces for the first `i` letters; `dp[0] = 0`, the rest start at `Infinity`.
2. For each `end` from 1 to `n`, reset `count`, `distinct` and `maxCount`.
3. Walk `start` from `end - 1` down to 0, adding `s[start]` to the counts and updating `distinct` and `maxCount`.
4. If `maxCount * distinct === end - start`, the piece is balanced, so try `dp[start] + 1` for `dp[end]`.
5. Return `dp[n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "fabccddg"`. The prefixes up to `"fabc"` have all-different letters, so `dp[1..4] = 1`. At `end = 5` the second `c` breaks that; a last piece `"c"` or `"cc"` gives `dp[5] = 2`. At `end = 6`, `"cd"` gives `dp[6] = dp[4] + 1 = 2`. At `end = 7`, walking left builds `"d"`, `"dd"`, `"cdd"`, `"ccdd"`; the last has `maxCount = 2`, `distinct = 2` and length 4, so `dp[7] = dp[3] + 1 = 2`. At `end = 8`, `"g"` and `"dg"` both give 3 and no longer piece is balanced, so the answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each (start, end) pair is visited once with O(1) work, plus 26 counters reset per `end`.
- Space: O(n) for `dp` and O(26) for `count`.

## Pitfalls

- Greedily taking the longest balanced first piece fails: `"aaabab"` becomes `"aaa"`, `"ba"`, `"b"` (3) while `"aa"`, `"abab"` needs 2.
- Letters absent from the piece do not count; comparing all 26 counters (zeros included) is wrong.
- Rebuilding the counts for every pair makes it O(n³); extend the piece one letter at a time.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[i]` | fewest balanced pieces for the first `i` letters |
| `end` | length of the prefix being solved |
| `start` | first index of the current last piece |
| `count` | letter counts inside `s[start..end)` |
| `distinct` | number of different letters in the piece |
| `maxCount` | largest letter count in the piece |
